paragraphs.text: Nanqiao was once the name of the county around [Mengzhe](nanqiao-ruigong-brick:nanqiao-name) in southern Yunnan. The Menghai County Nanqiao Tea Company, founded in February 2004, kept the old place name; its brand is Che Fo Nan, and its teas went to Hong Kong, Taiwan and Southeast Asia. Separately, at a [Malaysian tea fair](nanqiao-ruigong-brick:malaysian-tea-fair) in 2022, the exhibitor Quanyuxuan offered five Ruigong bricks together at stall 27, listed as ripe tea from 2008.

This brick is [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) from Menghai, made in 2009. The leaf was wetted and heaped in a covered [pile](shou:wet-piling), turned about once a week to spread the heat and let air in, then dried and pressed. At seventeen years it is well into what the trade counts as [aged ripe pu’er](shou:age-aged), and it is still changing slowly with the air and moisture around it, which is why storage shapes it as much as the years do.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.
